127.title: Sukkot: the booth
127.hook: a flimsy hut with a leafy roof, where people eat for a week under the stars
127.howItsDone: During Sukkot, many Jewish families build a sukkah with a roof of cut branches or reeds and eat their meals in it for seven days, some sleeping there too. Some welcome the ushpizin, biblical guests, along with real ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neilah: the last prayer of Yom Kippur, as the gates close. Your line was before the gates close. Five days after the fast, the mood flips.

Every fall, on certain streets, they appear: little huts on balconies, in backyards, in parking lots, even on apartment rooftops. Walls of canvas or plywood. A roof of palm fronds, bamboo mats or branches, with gaps you can see through. Paper chains and hanging fruit. A folding table inside, and a family eating dinner in their coats. Some even sleep out there. There's a custom of starting to build the night Yom Kippur ends, still tasting the first meal after the fast. For a week, the fanciest room in the house is a shack.
screen: `HUTS ON BALCONIES AND ROOFTOPS.` → `A ROOF OF BRANCHES.` → `DINNER IN YOUR COAT.`

segments.voice: The hut is a sukkah, and the holiday is Sukkot, the plural: booths. It begins on the fifteenth of the seventh month, under the full moon, and lasts seven days. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days," so each generation would remember that the Israelites lived in booths when they came out of Egypt. It's also a harvest festival, the last gathering of the year before the rains, and the Torah calls it a time to rejoice. The rabbis call it the season of our joy. The Talmud sets the minimum at two full walls and part of a third. It has to be temporary. And the roof must be things that grew from the ground and have been cut, like branches or reeds, thick enough for more shade than sun by day, and ideally loose enough to see the stars at night. So right after Yom Kippur, people move out of solid homes into something fragile. Why? The Talmud records two views of the booths in the wilderness: one rabbi says they were real huts, another says they were clouds of glory, God's protection overhead. Either way, a roof of branches becomes a way to remember being sheltered. There are guests too. Each night, some families welcome ushpizin: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph and David, and in some homes the women of the Bible as well, and real guests share the meal. And if it pours? The Mishnah says go inside. The sukkah is for joy, not misery.

segments.voice: Picture a meal outside, on a porch, a park bench or a step, under a roof of loose branches with the sky showing through. Think about what in your life is sturdier than it looks and what's more fragile than it looks, a job, a body, a friendship, and hold both kinds lightly. If you pray, you might give thanks for shelter.

Your line: live lightly for a week. A good meal needs less than you'd think. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: Sukkot: the four kinds (Leviticus 23:40)
128.hook: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, which midrash reads as four kinds of people held together
128.howItsDone: On each day of Sukkot except Shabbat, many Jews hold the lulav, myrtle and willow together with the etrog, say a blessing, and wave them in six directions, and carry them around the synagogue during the Hoshanot prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sukkah: a fragile hut with a roof of branches and stars. Your line was live lightly for a week. Today, what people hold in their hands in that hut.

On a Sukkot morning, someone stands in a sukkah holding what looks like a strange bouquet. In the right hand, a tall, closed palm branch, bound with sprigs of green leaves. In the left, a yellow fruit like a bumpy lemon, held so carefully you'd think it was glass. People pay real money for a perfect one. They say a blessing, bring both hands together, and wave the whole bundle: forward, to the side, behind, up, down. Gently, so the leaves rustle.
screen: `A STRANGE BOUQUET.` → `A LEMON HELD LIKE GLASS.` → `WAVED IN EVERY DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: It all comes from one verse. The Torah says that on the first day of the festival, "ye shall take you on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm-trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook," and rejoice. The rabbis identified the four: the etrog, a citron, for the goodly fruit; the lulav, a young palm branch; hadasim, myrtle, whose leaves grow thick and overlapping; and aravot, willows that grow by water. The whole bundle is often just called the lulav, after the tallest piece. Then the midrash asks: why these four? It answers by taste and smell. The etrog has both, like people who have both learning and good deeds. The palm's fruit, the date, has taste but no smell: learning without deeds. The myrtle has a lovely smell but no taste: good deeds without learning. And the willow has neither. What does God do with the willows? Throw them away? No. Bind them all into one bundle, and each makes up for the others. You can't do this mitzvah with three of the four. Leave out the plain willow and the whole thing doesn't count. Then the waving. Many wave toward all six directions: east, south, west, north, up and down. The Talmud explains it as waving to the One to whom every direction belongs, and as a way of holding back harmful winds and dews. And Sukkot sits right before the rainy season, so the willows of the brook join a festival that prays for rain.

Your line: every kind together. Even the plain willow belongs in the bundle. See you tomorrow.

129.title: Simchat Torah
129.hook: the reading finishes Deuteronomy and begins Genesis on the same day, with dancing
129.carry: finish and begin the same day
129.howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, synagogues take out all their Torah scrolls and dance with them in seven circuits called hakafot, read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis, and in many places call all the children up together under a prayer shawl.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lulav: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, bound together. Your line was every kind together.

Picture the most serious room you know, a place of quiet prayer, at its loudest. Every Torah scroll is out of the ark. People carry them in their arms like partners at a wedding, dancing in circles, singing, spilling into the street. Kids ride on shoulders waving flags. Someone's grandfather, who never dances, is dancing. A scroll gets passed to someone who's never held one. The circles go around seven times, and nobody's in a hurry. This is the last day of the fall holidays.
screen: `EVERY SCROLL OUT OF THE ARK.` → `DANCING WITH THE TORAH.` → `SEVEN TIMES AROUND.`

segments.voice: The day is called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah. It comes right after Sukkot: in Israel it's the same day as the festival called Shemini Atzeret; outside Israel it's the day after. Back on day twenty you met the scroll that never stays finished: the last lines of Deuteronomy, ending "in the sight of all Israel," and then at once, from a second scroll, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Today it happens, and the readers get honors. Their titles: the bridegroom of the Torah and the bridegroom of Genesis, and in many communities today, brides too. Then the dancing, the hakafot: seven circles around the reading table, every scroll in somebody's arms. Notice what nobody is doing. The scrolls stay closed, wrapped in their covers. No one is reading, explaining or being tested. People often point out that on this one day, the great scholar and the child who can't read a word are equal: all anyone is doing is holding the Torah and dancing. In many synagogues all the children are called up together under one big prayer shawl, spread over them like a canopy. The dancing turned up in unexpected places. In the Soviet Union in the 1960s, when religious life was pressed down hard, thousands of young Jews gathered in the street outside the Moscow synagogue on Simchat Torah night, singing and dancing. Many knew no Hebrew and none of the prayers. They knew the date. The writer Elie Wiesel went to see it and wrote about it in a book called The Jews of Silence. The joy is in holding the book, not in having mastered it.
screen: `THE BRIDEGROOMS OF TORAH AND GENESIS.` · `SEVEN CIRCLES, THE SCROLLS CLOSED.` · `THE CHILDREN UNDER ONE PRAYER SHAWL.` · `MOSCOW, THE 1960S: DANCING IN THE STREET.` · then, large: `HOLDING IT, NOT MASTERING IT.`

130.title: Hanukkah: the lights
130.hook: a small revolt, a rededicated Temple, and eight nights of lights in the window
130.howItsDone: For eight nights from the 25th of Kislev, Jewish families light a hanukkiah, adding one light each night with the shamash, say blessings, and place it in a window or doorway where passersby can see it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simchat Torah: dancing with the scrolls, ending Deuteronomy and beginning Genesis. Your line was finish and begin the same day. Now, a jump of two months, to the month of Kislev.

A winter evening, a street of lit windows. In some, a row of small flames: two, three, maybe eight, with one standing a little higher or off to the side. Candles in a silver holder, little cups of olive oil, a child's clay creation. They're not hidden in the dining room. They're in the window, facing the street, on purpose. Whoever lit them wants you, a stranger driving by, to see them. That's part of the point.
screen: `A ROW OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `PLACED IN THE WINDOW.` → `MEANT FOR STRANGERS TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Hanukkah means dedication. The story is told in the books of the Maccabees. The land of Israel was ruled by a Greek-speaking kingdom, and its king, Antiochus the Fourth, outlawed Jewish practice: Shabbat, circumcision, Torah study. The Temple in Jerusalem was turned over to the worship of other gods. A priestly family, led by an old man named Mattathias and then his son Judah, called the Maccabee, led a small revolt. Against the odds, they won back Jerusalem, cleaned the Temple, and rededicated it, on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev. Those books aren't part of the Hebrew Bible, and the festival isn't in the Torah: Hanukkah was set by the rabbis. Then the Talmud adds the oil. When the Temple was retaken, there was only one small jar of pure oil left, enough to light the Temple menorah for one day. It burned for eight. So Hanukkah lasts eight nights. And the Talmud gives the lights a job: to publicize the miracle. That's why they go in a doorway or a window facing the street, lit while people are still out walking. The lamp is often called a hanukkiah: eight lights, plus a helper light, the shamash, used to light the others. Hanukkah isn't one of the major holidays in Jewish law; work goes on as normal. But it's built to be seen. For a people once told not to be seen practicing, the whole mitzvah is to be seen.

131.title: Hanukkah: counting up (Shabbat 21b)
131.hook: Shammai said start with eight and go down; Hillel said start with one and go up, and Jews follow Hillel
131.howItsDone: Following the House of Hillel, Jews light one Hanukkah light on the first night and add one each night until eight, lighting the newest first with the shamash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lights of Hanukkah, placed in the window to be seen. Your line was add a light each night.

The first night, one candle, plus the helper. The second night, two. By the eighth, the whole row is blazing and the kids are counting out loud. The order looks obvious. In the Talmud's telling, it wasn't. Two schools of Jewish law looked at those same eight nights and disagreed. One said start full and go down. The other said start small and go up. Both gave reasons. Only one became the practice.
screen: `ONE CANDLE, THEN TWO, THEN EIGHT.` → `THE ORDER LOOKS OBVIOUS.` → `TWO SCHOOLS DISAGREED.`

segments.voice: The two schools were the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, the students of two famous teachers who lived around the time of Herod. They disagreed on many questions, and this is one. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, page twenty-one, lays it out. The House of Shammai said: on the first night, light eight, and each night, one fewer. The House of Hillel said: on the first night, light one, and each night, one more. Then come the reasons. Shammai's side said the lights should match the days still to come: eight days left, eight lights; one day left, one light. There's real sense in that. It's honest about time running out. Hillel's side gave a different kind of reason: in matters of holiness, we go up, and we don't go down. The Hebrew phrase is short, ma'alin ba-kodesh, we raise in holiness. And Jewish practice follows the House of Hillel, as the Talmud rules it generally should. Elsewhere the Talmud says why Hillel's school usually won: they were kind and humble, and they taught their opponents' views, even quoting Shammai's opinion before their own. Look at what that does to the eight nights. Shammai's way is a countdown; it ends small. Hillel's way is a count up; it ends with the most light. The argument is about candles, and also about which way a practice should move.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF SHAMMAI: EIGHT, THEN DOWN.` · `THE HOUSE OF HILLEL: ONE, THEN UP.` · `WE RAISE IN HOLINESS.` · `THE PRACTICE FOLLOWS HILLEL.` · then, large: `ALWAYS GO UP.`

segments.voice: Pick one tiny good thing to start with: a glass of water, a kind word, a page read, a minute of quiet. Not a countdown of things to give up, but a count up of things to add, so notice the empty space beside today's one thing, where tomorrow's will go.

132.title: Tu BiShvat
132.hook: the new year for trees, marked with fruits of the land of Israel
132.howItsDone: On Tu BiShvat, many Jews eat fruits, especially those the Torah links to the land of Israel, some hold a Tu BiShvat seder of fruits and wine, and many plant trees or support planting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's count: one light, then up to eight. Your line was always go up. Now, midwinter, a new year for trees.

The Talmud tells of a man named Honi. Walking along a road, he sees an old man planting a carob tree. Honi asks: how long until that tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the old man. Honi can't believe it: you think you'll live seventy more years to eat from it? The old man answers, more or less: I found this world full of carob trees. My grandparents planted them for me. So I'm planting this one for my grandchildren. Honi, the story goes, falls asleep for seventy years. When he wakes, a young man is picking carobs from that tree.
screen: `AN OLD MAN PLANTS A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO BEAR FRUIT.` → `PLANTED FOR THE GRANDCHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah lists four new years in the Jewish calendar, each with its own purpose; one is for trees. The House of Shammai said it falls on the first of the month of Shevat; the House of Hillel said the fifteenth, and again, Hillel's view is followed. In Hebrew, fifteen is written tet vav, which sounds like tu: Tu BiShvat, the fifteenth of Shevat. It began as a date for bookkeeping. The Torah has rules about fruit trees, how a tree's first years of fruit are left alone, and which year's produce is tithed, so you need a birthday to count a tree's age. The Talmud explains the date: by the fifteenth, most of the year's rain in the land of Israel has fallen, and the sap is rising. Over time, it became a celebration. Later, mystics following the Kabbalists of Safed shaped a Tu BiShvat seder: fruits and nuts eaten in a set order, and in one telling, cups of wine that move from white to red, like winter turning to spring. People eat the fruits the Torah praises in the land: "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey," a honey the rabbis read as date honey. In Israel and around the world, it's also a day for planting trees and caring for the earth. The Torah even forbids cutting fruit trees during a siege, asking: "for is the tree of the field man?" A tree can't run away. It's in your care.

133.title: Purim: Esther
133.hook: a queen, a villain and a hidden God whose name never appears in the book
133.howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, the megillah, both in the evening and again the next morning, often in costume.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees. Your line was a birthday for trees. Now, a month on in the calendar, a story read from a scroll.

Here's a story with everything. A king of Persia who throws a party for half a year. A queen who refuses his summons and is sent away. A beauty contest across the empire, won by a young Jewish woman who keeps her background secret, on her cousin's advice. A proud official who demands everyone bow to him, and when one Jew won't, plots to wipe out every Jew in the kingdom, and casts lots to pick the day. A sleepless king, a banquet, a sudden reversal. It reads like a palace thriller. And in the whole book, one name never appears.
screen: `A KING, A QUEEN, A SECRET.` → `A PLOT, AND LOTS CAST FOR A DAY.` → `ONE NAME NEVER APPEARS.`

segments.voice: The book is Esther, and on Purim it's read aloud from a handwritten scroll called the megillah. Megillah just means scroll, from a root meaning to roll. Purim means lots, the lots Haman cast to choose the day of destruction. And the name that never appears is God's. Not once. No miracles, no prophets, no voice from heaven. There's a queen who has to decide whether to risk her life by walking in to the king uninvited, and a cousin, Mordecai, who tells her that if she stays silent, help will come from somewhere else, and adds: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" She goes in. Everything turns. The Talmud plays on this. It hears in the name Esther the Hebrew for hidden, and links her to a verse in Deuteronomy where God says: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." So the book of Esther becomes the story of a hidden God. Not absent, hidden. Working through coincidences, a king's insomnia, a brave woman's choice. Some readers find ordinary life in this: no parted seas, just timing and courage, and, looking back, a pattern. One reason people give for Purim's costumes and masks: they hide who's underneath, the way God is hidden in the story. And look at this week: a hut of branches, four kinds bound together, dancing with the scrolls, lights in the window, a count going up, a tree's birthday, and now a hidden name.
